articles.author: johnettagaweraks
articles.description:
PHP2Shell makes runtime inventory the urgent patch problem


PHP is often treated as a dependency of an application rather than an internet-facing runtime. The October 2026 PHP2Shell release shows why that distinction breaks down. Two critical vulnerabilities in the PHP interpreter can lead to unauthenticated remote code execution under the right conditions, and the affected component may be present in containers, shared hosting, serverless images, and long-lived virtual machines.
The PHP project released fixes in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35 on October 21, 2026. The two vulnerabilities are CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Both are relevant to web applications because the interpreter processes request data before the application's own authorization logic has any chance to run…
articles.title: PHP2Shell makes runtime inventory the urgent patch problem

articles.author: Aqib Javaid
articles.description:
A dealer uploads a CSV with 500 rows. Each row is a SIM card that has to be activated on one of several carrier APIs, and each activation costs real wholesale money that you cannot get back if the row was bad. That was the shape of the bulk activation feature I built in Laravel for a wireless dealer platform, and it is a good test of what Laravel bulk CSV processing with queues actually requires once money and third-party APIs are involved.
Most tutorials stop at "chunk the file and dispatch a job per row". That is the easy 20%. The hard 80% is deciding what happens before the first row is touched, who pays while the job runs, what a retry is allowed to repeat, and how the user finds out what happened. Below are the five decisions I made on that project, what each one prevented, and the on…
articles.title: Laravel Bulk CSV Processing: Queues, Holds and Retries

articles.author: Mubeen Khan
articles.description:
Minification gets blamed for a lot of bugs it never caused. A script works fine in development, you run it through a minifier, and suddenly it throws in production. The minifier must have mangled something, right?
Most of the time, no. The minifier just removed the whitespace that was secretly holding your code together. The real culprit is automatic semicolon insertion, and it was already in your code, waiting.
JavaScript inserts semicolons for you when it thinks a statement has ended. That is convenient right up until a newline is the only thing separating two statements that should not be joined.
Take this:
const total = price + tax
(total > 100 ? applyDiscount() : checkout())

With the newline in place, JavaScript reads two statements. Now minify it by joining the lines:
const total = …
articles.title: Your minifier did not break your code. The missing semicolon did.

articles.description:
Your CRM says "St Josephs Med Ctr, 1 Main". Your vendor file says "Saint Joseph's Medical Center, 1 Main Street, Suite 200". A franchise list says "Store #4127". Are these the same real place? Exact string matching says no. Fuzzy matching says maybe. You want to know which business actually exists, and where.
Names come in with abbreviations, initialisms, store numbers, old spellings and "Inc" or "LLC" added or dropped. Addresses come in partial, with suite numbers in different fields, or as the registered office instead of the storefront. Comparing two strings can't tell you whether a business by that name really trades at that address today.
The reliable approach is to resolve each record against evidence about the place itself: its own website, map listings, social profiles, registries.…
